summary.text: Counting ordered pairs divisible by each power \(p^i\) gives the numerator valuation \(\sum_i\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor^2\), while Legendre’s formula gives the denominator valuation \(\sum_i\sum_{k\le \lfloor N/p^i\rfloor}k\lfloor\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor/k\rfloor\); the bound \(\sum_{k\le M}k\lfloor M/k\rfloor\le M^2\) also proves exact divisibility. Their difference depends only on \(\lfloor N/p\rfloor\), which is the same for \(N=np\) and \(N=np+k\) when \(k<p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
U(N)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{k=1}^{N}\gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D(N)=\prod_{k=1}^{N}\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor!\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
a(N)=\frac{U(N)}{D(N)}.
\]
We will first show that this quotient is an integer, and then compute enough of its prime factorization to prove the asserted constancy.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). All the factors occurring in \(U(N)\) and \(D(N)\) are positive, so both products are positive.

Fix a prime \(p\). Choose an integer \(B\) so large that
\[
N<p^B.
\]
All valuation sums below then terminate before \(B\).

First we calculate the valuation of the numerator. For \(1\le j,k\le N\), we have \(\gcd(j,k)<p^B\), and therefore
\[
v_p(\gcd(j,k))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid \gcd(j,k)}
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,p^i\mid k}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf 1_P\) is \(1\) when the condition \(P\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Summing over \(j\) and \(k\), and interchanging the finite sums, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(U(N))
&=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}v_p(\gcd(j,k))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
  \#\{1\le j\le N:p^i\mid j\}
  \#\{1\le k\le N:p^i\mid k\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The number of multiples of a positive integer \(d\) among \(1,\dots,N\) is \(\lfloor N/d\rfloor\). Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(U(N))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]

We next calculate the denominator valuation. By additivity of valuations on products and the identity \(v_p(x^k)=k v_p(x)\),
\[
v_p(D(N))
 =\sum_{k=1}^{N} k\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor!\right).
\]
Legendre's formula says that, for every nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(\lfloor N/k\rfloor\le N<p^B\), all terms with \(i\ge B\) vanish. Hence
\[
v_p(D(N))
 =\sum_{k=1}^{N}k\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
For integer quotients,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor N/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N}{kp^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor
   \frac{\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor}{k}
  \right\rfloor.
\]
After interchanging the finite sums, set
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then
\[
v_p(D(N))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{k=1}^{N}
 k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(k>M_i\), the inner quotient is zero. Since \(M_i\le N\), the range of the inner sum may therefore be shortened from \(1\le k\le N\) to \(1\le k\le M_i\). Thus
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(D(N))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{k=1}^{M_i}
 k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{2}
\]

We now prove that \(D(N)\mid U(N)\), so that the displayed ratio defining \(a(N)\) is exact. For every nonnegative integer \(M\) and each \(1\le k\le M\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac Mk\right\rfloor\le M.
\]
There are \(M\) terms, and hence
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{M}k\left\lfloor\frac Mk\right\rfloor\le M^2.
\tag{3}
\]
Apply this with \(M=M_i\) in (2). Comparing with (1) gives
\[
v_p(D(N))
 \le \sum_{i=1}^{B-1}M_i^2
 =v_p(U(N)).
\]
This argument applies to every prime \(p\). Since \(U(N)\) and \(D(N)\) are positive integers, the prime-factorization criterion for divisibility now yields
\[
D(N)\mid U(N).
\]
Therefore \(a(N)=U(N)/D(N)\) is an integer, and for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(a(N))=v_p(U(N))-v_p(D(N)).
\tag{4}
\]

The crucial consequence of formulas (1) and (2) is the following.

**Claim.** If \(N\) and \(M\) are nonnegative integers satisfying
\[
\left\lfloor\frac Np\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac Mp\right\rfloor,
\tag{5}
\]
then
\[
v_p(a(N))=v_p(a(M)).
\]

To prove the claim, choose one common \(B\) sufficiently large that both \(N<p^B\) and \(M<p^B\). For every \(i\ge1\), write \(i=r+1\). Associativity of integer division gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor
   \frac{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{p^r}
  \right\rfloor,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor
   \frac{\lfloor M/p\rfloor}{p^r}
  \right\rfloor.
\]
By (5), these quantities are equal for every \(i\ge1\). In other words, all the values
\[
M_i=\left\lfloor\frac{N}{p^i}\right\rfloor
\]
appearing in (1) and (2) agree with their counterparts for \(M\). Formula (1) therefore gives
\[
v_p(U(N))=v_p(U(M)),
\]
and formula (2) gives
\[
v_p(D(N))=v_p(D(M)).
\]
Subtracting according to (4) proves the claim.

We finally apply the claim to the required consecutive block. Let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy \(0\le k<p\). Since a prime is positive, Euclidean division gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor=n.
\]
Also,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor
 =n+\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p}\right\rfloor
 =n,
\]
because \(0\le k<p\). Thus \(np\) and \(np+k\) satisfy condition (5), and the claim yields
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k)).
\]
This holds for every \(k=0,1,\dots,p-1\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
 =\cdots
 =\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
which is precisely conjecture C for A129365.
